How-Tos.name: How-Tos
How-Tos.heading: How-Tos
How-Tos.fit: framing a familiar challenge for idea generation; participants need knowledge of the problem and its stakeholders.
How-Tos.input: short problem statement plus stakeholders and relevant product/service life phases.
How-Tos.core: identify stakeholders and aspects; generate multiple action-oriented How-To questions; regroup questions to understand common themes; choose questions spanning perspectives; generate ideas against each chosen question.
How-Tos.output: a set of useful question frames and ideas linked to them.
How-Tos.consideration: move between concrete and abstract framing when ideas stall; do not let selection of frames erase stakeholder diversity.
How-Tos.planningEstimate: allocate time for question generation and selection before the subsequent idea generation. Avoid presenting the complete process as a quick prompt rewrite.
How-Tos.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · How-Tos · verified record: Core

Braindrawing.name: Braindrawing
Braindrawing.heading: Braindrawing
Braindrawing.fit: making ideas visible and developing each other's concepts; typically produces fewer, richer ideas than brainwriting.
Braindrawing.input: a clear concrete target or initial ideas.
Braindrawing.core: clarify the challenge and divergent rules; each person sketches; pass sheets after a few minutes so others add or create variants; repeat; explain/title the sketches for shared understanding; select promising ideas using criteria.
Braindrawing.output: developed sketches ready for selection or further design.
Braindrawing.consideration: reassure hesitant drawers; quality of the drawing is secondary to the communicated idea.
Braindrawing.planningEstimate: budget each pass, subsequent explanation, and selection. A remote shared-board version is an adaptation and needs explicit turn-taking.
Braindrawing.sourceGroup: 4–8 people, A3 sheets, legible dark markers.
Braindrawing.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · Braindrawing · verified record: Core

Morphological Chart.name: Morphological Chart
Morphological Chart.heading: Morphological Chart
Morphological Chart.fit: systematically combining solutions where a clear main function can be divided into sub-functions; requires analytical framing.
Morphological Chart.input: main function, sub-functions, and design requirements.
Morphological Chart.core: list sub-functions as rows; generate candidate solutions per row; form combinations taking one solution from each row; assess against requirements; choose at least three principal solutions; sketch and elaborate selected combinations.
Morphological Chart.output: alternative complete solution concepts assembled from component choices.
Morphological Chart.consideration: combinations grow rapidly; reduce and group options before combining. For services with no clear main function, choose a less systematic method.
Morphological Chart.planningEstimate: prepare or validate the functional decomposition before expecting participants to produce coherent combinations.
Morphological Chart.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · Morphological Chart · verified record: Core

SCAMPER.name: SCAMPER
SCAMPER.heading: SCAMPER
SCAMPER.fit: extending or changing existing ideas when initial generation slows.
SCAMPER.input: an existing idea, concept, or product.
SCAMPER.core: explore substitution, combination, adaptation, modification, alternative use, elimination, and reversal; capture variations; regroup for understanding; select promising directions for development.
SCAMPER.output: new variants or stepping stones from existing concepts.
SCAMPER.consideration: delay criticism of unusual ideas. The source cautions that inexperienced designers may need support.
SCAMPER.planningEstimate: demonstrate one prompt and explain that different prompts will yield different amounts of useful material. Selecting only some prompts is an adaptation.
SCAMPER.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · SCAMPER · verified record: Core

C-Box.name: C-Box
C-Box.heading: C-Box
C-Box.fit: understanding and evaluating a large early idea set without automatically discarding novelty.
C-Box.input: roughly 10–60 ideas on movable notes, according to the source.
C-Box.core: define novelty and feasibility axes; review and place ideas together; reflect on gaps; either develop difficult ideas toward feasibility, generate ideas in gaps, or select promising ideas.
C-Box.output: a shared map and a direction for development or selection.
C-Box.consideration: proximity on the map does not establish similarity; interesting but difficult ideas may deserve development.
C-Box.planningEstimate: clarify how feasibility will be judged. Mapping, discussion, and selection are separate time demands. Other axes are an explicitly named adaptation.
C-Box.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · C-Box · verified record: Core

Harris Profile.name: Harris Profile
Harris Profile.heading: Harris Profile
Harris Profile.fit: making concept evaluations explicit and discussable when requirements exist but precise performance data may not.
Harris Profile.core: create a four-position scale for each requirement; evaluate each concept; fill a visual profile; present profiles together and discuss implications.
Harris Profile.output: comparable visual profiles and a reasoned discussion about concepts to explore.
Harris Profile.consideration: define scale meanings per criterion. This is an intuitive visual assessment, not a precise calculation; requirements can evolve during discussion.
Harris Profile.planningEstimate: reserve time to agree scale meanings before scoring.
Harris Profile.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · Harris Profile · verified record: Core

Datum Method.name: Datum Method
Datum Method.heading: Datum Method
Datum Method.fit: comparing concepts developed to a similar level against explicit criteria.
Datum Method.input: comparable proposals, criteria, and a chosen reference concept.
Datum Method.core: build a matrix; choose a datum; compare each alternative as worse, same, or better on each criterion; discuss results; use another strong datum and iterate toward a reasoned choice; drop weak designs when appropriate.
Datum Method.output: comparisons, clarified strengths/weaknesses, and a selection for development.
Datum Method.consideration: the method aids decisions rather than mathematically proving them. Vague criteria can obscure meaningful differences.
Datum Method.planningEstimate: budget a bounded number of comparison rounds and protect discussion; do not promise automatic consensus.
Datum Method.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · Datum Method · verified record: Core

Weighted Objectives.name: Weighted Objectives
Weighted Objectives.heading: Weighted Objectives
Weighted Objectives.fit: selecting among a few developed alternatives with enough information for systematic evaluation.
Weighted Objectives.core: agree criteria and weights; build a matrix; score concepts against criteria; calculate weighted totals; discuss the preferred concept and review weights/scores.
Weighted Objectives.output: an explicit weighted comparison supporting a decision.
Weighted Objectives.consideration: small numerical differences may not be meaningful; a lower-scoring concept can retain greater development potential.
Weighted Objectives.planningEstimate: agree scoring anchors and reserve discussion for close results. Calculate weighted sums consistently rather than treating rankings as objective proof.
Weighted Objectives.citation: Delft Design Guide · Methods: Develop & Deliver · Weighted Objectives · verified record: Core

frameworks.name: Reasoning in design
frameworks.source: Delft Design Guide · Planning models · Reasoning in design
notes: Source category: Model of design reasoning, not a session timetable.
Fit: structuring insights, generating questions, communicating reasoning, and reflecting on how a proposed form addresses needs and values. Primarily product-oriented but applicable to services.
Source How headings: Form; Properties; Function; Needs and Values. These are components, not numbered stages.
Analysis: reason from form, properties, and usage context toward predicted functioning and consequences.
Synthesis: reason from user values and needs toward functions, properties, and a suitable form. The diagram identifies these as deductive analysis and abductive synthesis.
Output: explicit relationships connecting proposed form and material, properties, functions, needs, and values, with mode and conditions of use considered.

Constraints: consider usage context as carefully as the product. Properties can have desirable and undesirable consequences; intended functions can differ from uses people discover. Intuition and creativity remain necessary.

Application (facilitator adaptation): a mapping exercise must cite the selected How components and the analysis/synthesis direction used. Its prompts, grouping, and time allocation are adaptations, not source-prescribed instructions.

frameworks.name: Basic Design Cycle
frameworks.source: Delft Design Guide · Planning models · Basic Design Cycle
notes: Source category: Model of iterative reasoning. Its five reasoning steps are not five project phases and must not be presented as a one-pass project timeline.
Fit: examining whether a design process has skipped necessary reasoning; organizing thought, action, evaluation, and decisions at different levels of detail.
Source How headings and corresponding diagram outputs:
1. Analyse: examine the goal/problem and relevant aspects, informing criteria and requirements. Diagram output: Criteria.
2. Synthesis: generate possible solutions or elements of proposals. Diagram output: Provisional Design.
3. Simulate: create imagined, digital, or physical representations of proposals so their consequences can be considered. Diagram output: Expected Properties.
4. Evaluate: assess potential value through those representations against design criteria. Diagram output: Value of the Design.
5. Decide: judge relative value and choose whether to proceed, repeat, or focus on other elements. Diagram output: Approved Design, with iteration possible.
The numbered mapping above corresponds to the diagram; the text itself uses heading labels. Use the exact heading as the reference when documenting a borrowed reasoning step.

Constraints: a cycle may occur within seconds or over weeks. Entry can be at different points, but complete the reasoning cycle. Reflect and discuss missing steps rather than jumping directly to solutions.

Application (facilitator adaptation): use this model to check a proposed session sequence. A session may only advance part of a larger cycle; identify what was completed and what must happen after the session. Do not claim a short session produces an approved design simply because it includes Decide.

frameworks.name: Design Drawing as a Language
frameworks.source: Delft Design Guide · Perspectives · Design Drawing as a Language
notes: Source category: Perspective, not a fixed numbered workshop exercise.
Fit: visual exploration and communication throughout designing; supports developing thoughts, exchanging ideas, and discussing proposals with others.
Source headings: What & Why; Mindset; How; Tips & Concerns; Limitations. The source gives no numbered procedure, fixed duration, or participant count.

Core guidance: use drawing to externalize observations and concepts; tailor the representation to purpose, audience, decision, information flow, and design stage. The How section relates drawing to Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver and points to the stage-specific drawing methods elsewhere in the book.

Constraints: drawing takes practice. Begin with basic shapes and gradually increase complexity; choose clear composition, viewpoints, lines, and tonal values. Later work may require other formats, often preceded by sketches.

Application (facilitator adaptation): when drawing becomes an actual activity, select and read the relevant named stage-specific drawing method. Reference this perspective for the rationale and that method for its steps; do not invent numbered steps and attribute them to this perspective.

guidance.title: Outcome first
notes: Translate the creative challenge into a concrete end product: e.g. a clarified opportunity, a diverse set of concepts, developed concept sketches, or a shortlist with owners. Identify which stages are needed to reach it. A useful sequence may move through framing, divergence, development, and convergence, but do not force every stage into every session.

Compare candidates on purpose, prerequisites, usable output, participant experience, group size, available tools, inclusion, energy, and complete delivery time. Explain the decisive reasons for the selected activities. Mention a rejected alternative only when it helps the user understand a real tradeoff.

guidance.title: Connect the sequence
notes: For each stage, name the input and output and verify the next stage can consume it. Reserve time to consolidate raw ideas before selecting. Agree selection criteria before voting or evaluation. State who can decide and whether a vote is advisory or binding.

Adapt reporting to scale. Calculate serial sharing explicitly; use pairs, table representatives, a gallery, or written clustering when a full round would consume the session. Account for the synthesis work those alternatives still require.

Use quiet individual work when it improves participation before group discussion. Give accessible alternatives to movement, rapid drawing, or speaking on demand when relevant. Make remote instructions and capture locations explicit. Treat energy changes as design choices, not as reasons to add unrelated games.

guidance.title: Feasibility
notes: A candidate's quoted activity duration may exclude explanation, grouping, sharing, or debrief. Estimate its full footprint before selecting it. If an adaptation removes a central step or materially changes the intended result, name it as an adapted exercise rather than representing it as the original method.

Keep a fallback only for plausible friction: unclear prompt, low idea volume, disagreement, technology failure, or overrun. Specify the trigger and response. Fallbacks should preserve the objective while simplifying mechanics.

guidance.title: Build the time budget
notes: Compute the available minutes from start and end, or the supplied total duration. Deduct fixed opening, breaks, closure, and contingency before allocating activity time. Include any lunch or required interruption. Ask for a timezone only when coordinating participants across locations or dates.

For each activity, budget explanation and demonstration, setup/grouping, individual work, group work, reporting, and synthesis/debrief. Internal components must sum to the activity row; do not count them twice. Give transitions separate rows for moving people, changing materials, opening boards, and carrying outputs forward.
Working estimates to adjust:
- A simple instruction: 2–4 minutes; unfamiliar multistep activity: 5–8 minutes including an example and understanding check.
- A simple transition: 2–3 minutes; movement, regrouping, or board changes: 4–7 minutes.
- Reporting: number of speakers × speaking allowance, plus handoffs and synthesis. Eight tables at 2 minutes each require at least 16 minutes before handoffs or synthesis.

- For sustained sessions, normally provide a 10–15 minute break after roughly 60–90 minutes of demanding work. Adjust for accessibility, energy, format, and the user's constraints. A brief reset may suffice in a short session; do not add a long break mechanically.
- Reserve about 5–10% of the total window as explicit contingency, more when conditions are uncertain. If the window is very short, use a small stated buffer and fewer activities.
- Protect enough closing time to capture decisions, owners, and next steps; commonly 5–10 minutes, longer for complex commitments.

guidance.title: Arithmetic check
notes: Use one time system consistently, preferably start/end clock times plus duration. Every row starts when the previous row ends. Sum durations and verify the final end matches the hard stop. Breaks, transitions, and buffer are part of the total. For each activity, also check its component budget. Report the total and whether all rows fit.

Use realistic numbers rather than implying that estimates guarantee completion. Name assumptions that affect timing, especially participant count, number of reports, and complexity of the task. A schedule needing more time than the window is infeasible even if its individual activities sound reasonable.

guidance.title: Recovery during delivery
notes: At checkpoints, compare actual progress with the run sheet. Spend the stated buffer first when that is appropriate. Then shorten optional reporting, reduce the number of ideas developed, or remove a lower-priority activity. Keep essential synthesis, decisions, breaks, and closure where possible. State the lost scope or output and issue a revised remaining schedule.

Do not recover an overrun by accelerating unfamiliar instructions or assuming everyone will work faster. If the core deliverable no longer fits, offer an achievable reduced deliverable and identify what needs follow-up.
